overview: SR Bancorp, Inc. is the Maryland-incorporated holding company for Somerset Regal Bank, a 138-year-old New Jersey state-chartered commercial bank formed via the September 2023 mutual-to-stock conversion of Somerset Savings Bank combined with the simultaneous cash acquisition of Regal Bancorp. The bank operates 14 full-service branches across affluent central and northern New Jersey counties (Essex, Hunterdon, Middlesex, Morris, Somerset and Union), with roughly $960 million in total assets, ~$800 million in loans and ~$846 million in deposits as of June 30, 2025. It is a micro-cap thrift-turned-commercial-bank (~9M shares, ~$180M market cap) trading close to tangible book value.

business_model.description: Classic community bank spread-lending model: gathers low-cost core deposits (checking, savings, money market, CDs) from a six-county New Jersey franchise and redeploys them into residential mortgages, multi-family, commercial real estate, C&I (including SBA) and consumer loans. Revenue is overwhelmingly net interest income (spread between loan/investment yields and deposit/borrowing costs) supplemented by modest noninterest income (fees, BOLI income). No brokered deposits are used. Historically a residential-mortgage-heavy thrift, the bank is deliberately shifting mix toward higher-yielding multi-family and commercial real estate following the 2023 Regal Bank merger, which brought meaningful commercial lending capability.

revenue_streams.name: Residential mortgage loans
revenue_streams.description: One-to-four family fixed and adjustable-rate mortgages; 53.4% of loan portfolio at 6/30/25; ~42% of originations sourced via third-party mortgage brokers

revenue_streams.name: Multi-family real estate loans
revenue_streams.description: 5+ unit rental properties, adjustable rate tied to 5-yr UST; fastest-growing segment, 100% broker-referred originations; 27.5% of loan book at 6/30/25 (up from 24.5% a year prior)

revenue_streams.name: Commercial real estate (owner-occupied and other)
revenue_streams.description: Office, industrial, retail and other commercial properties in-market

revenue_streams.name: Commercial & Industrial / SBA loans
revenue_streams.description: Working capital and equipment loans to small/medium local businesses, largely via SBA program

revenue_streams.name: Consumer & other loans
revenue_streams.description: Home equity loans/lines, small unsecured personal and rehab loans

revenue_streams.name: Investment securities income
revenue_streams.description: Held-to-maturity portfolio (~$142M) of agency MBS, subordinated debentures and CMOs used for liquidity/collateral, not a primary earnings driver

business_model.customer_type: Primarily retail/consumer depositors and borrowers (B2C) with a growing small-business/commercial (B2B/SMB) segment; local municipal deposit relationships ($31.8M) also present
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Jersey — concentrated in Essex, Hunterdon, Middlesex, Morris, Somerset and Union counties; no meaningful geographic diversification

competitive_position.market_position: Small, sub-scale community bank with limited market share (e.g., 2.1% deposit share in its home Somerset County, ranked 9th of 20 institutions). Competes against much larger regional/national banks, other thrifts, credit unions, and non-bank/fintech lenders in an intensely competitive, affluent New Jersey market.
moat_factors: 138-year local operating history and community bank reputation/trust in its NJ market area
Relatively affluent, economically diverse market footprint (pharma, life sciences, financial services, tech, logistics employers) supporting stable deposit and loan demand
No brokered deposits and low reliance on wholesale funding to date, supporting a lower-cost, sticky core deposit base
Well-capitalized / overcapitalized balance sheet post-IPO gives flexibility for opportunistic buybacks and potential bolt-on M&A
competitive_threats: Sub-scale asset base (~$1B) versus larger regional banks with far greater marketing, technology and pricing resources
Heavy reliance on third-party mortgage brokers for residential (42%) and 100% of multi-family originations, a relationship that could be disrupted
Intense deposit competition pressuring cost of funds (interest-bearing deposit costs rose from 1.13% to 1.88% YoY at FY25)
Fintech and non-bank lenders lowering barriers to entry in mortgage and consumer lending
Limited brand recognition/scale to win larger commercial relationships against bigger regional competitors

business: Geographic concentration risk — virtually all loans secured by NJ real estate; no geographic diversification cushion against a local downturn
Shift toward multi-family/CRE and C&I lending increases credit risk relative to the bank's historical residential mortgage profile

Heavy reliance on third-party brokers for loan origination (42% of residential purchases, 100% of multi-family originations in FY25); discontinuation of these relationships would hurt origination volume
Key person / management transition risk following the January 1, 2026 CEO change (42-year veteran William Taylor retired, succeeded by Christopher Pribula)

Vendor data security incident (disclosed July 2026, via accounting vendor Mercadien) exposed customer PII (names, SSNs, account numbers, IDs); reputational/regulatory risk even though core banking systems were unaffected
Material weakness in internal controls identified at 6/30/25 related to untimely recognition of BOLI income from a former employee's death, raising financial reporting execution risk
Small scale limits ability to compete on technology, pricing and marketing versus larger banks
financial: Low profitability — ROA ~0.4% and ROE roughly low-single-digits, well below peer community banks (e.g., Unity Bancorp ~17% ROE, Parke Bancorp ~11% ROE), reflecting post-conversion excess capital and merger-related drag
Elevated wholesale/time-deposit reliance — CDs were 31.7% of deposits at FY25, with $239M (28.3% of total deposits) maturing within one year, creating repricing risk in a competitive rate environment
Uninsured deposits grew to $145.3M (up from $109.7M YoY), a liquidity risk in a stress scenario
Net interest margin sensitivity to interest rate/yield curve shifts given asset-liability duration mismatch typical of thrifts
Overcapitalization is dilutive to ROE — proceeds from the 2023 IPO have not yet been fully deployed into higher-earning assets
regulatory: Extensive dual regulation by the NJDBI and FDIC (bank level) and the Federal Reserve (holding company level), with discretion over capital distributions, growth and M&A approvals

Post-conversion regulatory constraints — as a recently converted thrift holding company, capital return and change-of-control activity are subject to added regulatory scrutiny; the standard 3-year anti-takeover moratorium from the September 2023 conversion expires September 2026, after which acquisition activity becomes easier to pursue/receive
Federal Reserve/FDIC approval required for buybacks exceeding 10% of consolidated net worth in a 12-month period and for dividend increases exceeding retained earnings
CRA, BSA/AML and consumer compliance costs typical of community banks; last CRA rating 'Satisfactory' (April 2025)
Data security incident could draw regulatory/consumer-protection scrutiny despite management's view of no material financial impact
macro: Interest rate risk — profitability tied to net interest margin, which is sensitive to Fed policy, yield curve shape and deposit repricing lags
Local/regional economic sensitivity — NJ real estate values and employment conditions directly drive loan performance given near-total real estate collateralization (98.5% of loans)
Inflation and tariff-driven cost pressure on local business borrowers cited explicitly as a risk factor in the FY25 10-K
Broader recession risk could raise delinquencies/non-performing assets despite currently pristine credit quality (near-zero NPAs)

growth_drivers: Continued mix-shift toward higher-yielding multi-family, commercial real estate and C&I lending to lift net interest margin and ROA/ROE off currently depressed post-conversion levels
Full deployment of excess IPO capital into earning assets, which should mechanically improve returns as the balance sheet normalizes

Capital return program — three successive stock buyback authorizations since 2023 (most recently May 2026, ~801,320 shares / 10% of shares outstanding) executed at/below tangible book value, directly accretive to book value per share and EPS
Newly initiated/growing dividend — 20% increase announced June 2026 to $0.06/quarter, signaling confidence in earnings trajectory and capital strength
New CEO (Christopher Pribula, effective Jan 1, 2026) may bring renewed strategic focus on commercial banking build-out and profitability improvement

Potential sale/merger optionality — the 3-year post-conversion acquisition moratorium expires September 2026; recently converted, overcapitalized thrifts like SRBK are classic consolidation targets once that restriction lifts
Opportunistic bolt-on M&A given excess capital position, following the successful 2023 Regal Bank integration playbook

recent_developments.event: CEO William P. Taylor (42-year veteran) announced retirement effective January 1, 2026; Christopher J. Pribula named successor as President & CEO of both SR Bancorp and Somerset Regal Bank
CEO transition completed; Taylor remains as director and Executive Chairman

bull_case: Trades near or below tangible book value (~0.7-0.9x P/TBV per third-party estimates) while sitting on excess post-IPO capital, providing meaningful downside cushion and buyback accretion
Improving profitability trend — Q3 FY2026 net income up 65% YoY and NIM expanding, suggesting the post-conversion earnings drag is fading as capital gets deployed into higher-yielding loans
Three consecutive share buyback programs plus a newly-raised dividend demonstrate management/board commitment to shareholder capital return and confidence in the balance sheet
Pristine current credit quality (essentially zero non-performing loans/assets, no troubled debt restructurings) provides a clean base heading into a period of loan mix diversification

September 2026 expiration of the standard 3-year post-conversion acquisition moratorium opens the door to takeover speculation — thrift conversions historically trade up on M&A optionality once this restriction lifts, and an overcapitalized ~$1B NJ bank in an affluent market is a plausible target for larger regional acquirers
bear_case: Profitability remains weak on an absolute basis — ROA near 0.4% and ROE in the low single digits are far below profitable community bank peers, and there's no guarantee the improvement trend continues or accelerates enough to close the gap
Sub-scale franchise (~$1B assets, 14 branches, single-state) faces structural cost and pricing disadvantages against larger, better-capitalized regional banks and non-bank lenders
Concentrated NJ real estate collateral (98.5% of loans) and rising CRE/multi-family mix increase cyclicality and credit risk exposure versus the bank's historically conservative residential book

Newly disclosed vendor data breach and a previously identified material weakness in internal controls (BOLI income recognition) raise execution and reputational risk concerns for a small-cap name with limited resources to absorb missteps

M&A/sale speculation is unconfirmed — no announced merger or acquisition has been disclosed as of mid-2026; investors buying purely on takeout optionality risk disappointment if a deal does not materialize post-moratorium, leaving the stock dependent on organic profitability improvement alone
analyst_notes: SRBK is a textbook recently-converted thrift trading close to tangible book value (roughly 0.7x-0.9x P/TBV per third-party estimates, with reported TBV/share around $19 versus a ~$19.65 stock price), reflecting the market's skepticism about near-term ROE given the excess capital raised in the September 2023 mutual-to-stock conversion/Regal Bank merger. Consistent with typical thrift-conversion dynamics, management has prioritized capital return: three buyback authorizations since IPO (totaling well over 20% of the original share count) plus a newly-initiated and recently-increased dividend (20% hike to $0.06/quarter in June 2026). No confirmed M&A/sale announcement has been identified as of this writing (through the July 2026 8-Ks reviewed, which cover a data-security vendor incident rather than a corporate transaction) — searches did not surface any Stilwell Group, Seidman, or other named thrift-activist 13D filings against SRBK; the only notable holder identified is the company's own ESOP trust (~9% passive stake per a February 2026 13G). That said, the structural setup is exactly the kind of situation thrift-conversion investors watch closely: the standard 3-year post-conversion acquisition/control moratorium expires in September 2026, at which point SRBK becomes eligible to be acquired without the regulatory friction that applies during the moratorium period, and overcapitalized, sub-scale, recently-converted NJ thrifts have historically been frequent acquisition targets in the 3-5 year window after conversion. Investors should watch for (1) 13D filings from known thrift activists after September 2026, (2) further upward earnings/NIM trends validating the capital-deployment thesis, and (3) any strategic-alternatives language in future earnings calls or proxy materials. Until/unless a deal emerges, the investment case rests on continued organic ROE improvement plus buyback/dividend-driven capital return, with takeover potential as a call option rather than a base-case catalyst.
